claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a reported hierarchical heterostructure with multilevel chemical fluctuations.
Binary-phase-diagram-derived parameters can be used as inputs to a machine-learning framework for high-entropy alloys.
Binary subsystem parameters can represent the local chemical environments in hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed framework can predict Young's modulus for hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed framework can predict yield strength for hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed framework can predict fracture toughness for hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
The hierarchical heterostructure mediates mechanical properties through locally varying chemical interactions.
Phase-diagram-inspired parameters effectively encapsulate the locally varying chemical interactions in the heterostructure.
Encoding binary thermodynamic interactions in reduced parameters can bypass detailed multiscale calculations.
Microscale phase behavior encoded by the reduced parameters can be linked directly to macroscopic mechanical response.
The framework will reduce computational time by 80–90% relative to CALPHAD and first-principles methods.
The framework will improve mechanical-property prediction accuracy by approximately 5–10% in terms of error margins.
Direct CALPHAD, first-principles, and high-fidelity machine-learning methods require significant computational resources.
Existing high-fidelity methods have limited predictive capability for fracture toughness.
The approach may become unreliable when multibody or higher-order interactions dominate beyond the binary approximation.
Computational gains and prediction-error improvements depend on how representative the binary parameters are of multicomponent interactions.
Reduced binary-derived parameters may inadequately capture fracture mechanisms.
A blinded prospective benchmark will treat greater than 10% error for any target property or less than a fivefold computational improvement as falsifying outcomes.
